A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Sandwich BNN research. All 15 pages of v2 and 18 pages of v3, including their appendices, support comparison; retained equations, tables, and figures can be matched across renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original ACOPF experiments on 57-, 118-, 500-, and 2000-bus systems, including optimization errors and empirical confidence-bound analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experiments and adds repeated-trial case118 sensitivity studies and original results on two synthetic non-OPF problem configurations.

M1.justification: The alternating supervised/feasibility training, BNN architecture, likelihoods, posterior sampling, and Selection via Posterior procedure remain unchanged. The new experiments apply existing methods without documenting a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates only ACOPF problems. v3 Appendix D adds a distinct synthetic optimization task with a quadratic and sinusoidal objective and linear constraints, using 20- and 70-variable configurations. This materially extends evaluation beyond power grids; all original ACOPF coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The original ACOPF comparisons retain the same BNN variants, Sandwich DNN, Naive MAE/MSE, penalty methods, and LD+MAE. New studies reuse existing supervised and Sandwich BNN comparators. Donti et al. supplies the synthetic benchmark; DC3 is not newly evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: v3 adds a case118 evaluation grid with 512, 1024, and 2048 labeled samples, 2048 fixed unlabeled samples, and 10- or 15-minute budgets. The non-OPF experiments use 4096 supervised samples, 512 unsupervised samples, 100 test instances, and 400- or 800-second budgets. These are additional protocols, not replacements for the original settings. Section 5's '5048' conflicts with the consistently reported 2048 in the appendix.

E4.justification: New Appendix C systematically examines sensitivity to labeled-data size and training time, comparing supervised and Sandwich BNNs with and without SvP. Tables 6–7 and Figures 5 and 8–15 add substantial evidence about resource sensitivity and stability. The original component comparisons and posterior/test-sample convergence analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 reports selecting the best model from five trials. v3 retains that practice for the original results but adds five-trial means and minimum–maximum displays for the sensitivity study, plus three-run averages for the non-OPF experiment. This substantially expands reporting of variation between trials; it does not establish an increased run count for the original experiments.

E6.justification: The original ACOPF numerical tables are unchanged after matching renumbered tables. v3 adds the resource-sensitivity results and Table 10's synthetic results. For the new 70-variable comparison, Sandwich BNN reports maximum equality violation 0.298 versus supervised BNN's 0.484 and inequality violation 0.109 versus 0.170, but a worse cost gap, 7.1% versus 2.6%. These are new findings, not same-setting improvements over v2.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds the mathematical definition of the synthetic optimization problem in Equation (6). The existing feasibility assumptions, BNN derivations, variance hypothesis, and concentration inequalities are unchanged; v2's Theorems D.1–D.3 become E.1–E.3 without new proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same scientific contributions: Sandwich BNN training under limited resources, improved feasibility relative to DNN approaches, and confidence bounds using predictive variance. The abstract adds code-access information, while the additional experiments support existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations that larger datasets require longer training, supervised BNNs offer more predictable outcomes, and residual inequality errors are harder to suppress. Existing large-system limitations remain. Some new interpretations are inconsistent with the evidence: Appendix C describes increasing maximum equality errors although Figure 5 and Table 6 show decreases.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the supplementary ZIP and promised future release description with BNN-OPF repository access information. It also identifies the new studies' Mac Mini M4 with 24 GB RAM and Xeon 2.20 GHz hardware, and attributes synthetic-data generation to Donti et al.'s code. Original Appendix B implementation details remain unchanged; repository contents were not inspected.

R1.justification: The cited-work set and substantive novelty positioning remain unchanged. Khadivi and Sharma references are updated from preprints to publications of the same works. The new experiment reuses the already cited Donti benchmark without introducing a new competing method or revising the related-work argument.

P1.justification: v3 expands the numerical discussion and locally reorganizes the appendices: robustness becomes Appendix C, retained larger-system results become C.1, and concentration bounds move to E around the new Appendix D. There are also limited copyedits, author-order changes, and publication-header updates; most existing prose is retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds a comparative error-bar figure, eight detailed sensitivity figures, two tables organized by model and training budget, and the synthetic-results table. This substantially expands the visual evidence. Original figures and tables are retained, with appendix renumbering and relocation rather than substantive redraws.

improvement.justification: Adding trial means and ranges addresses v2's limited visibility into variability beyond its best-of-five results. The non-OPF experiment and clearer code-access information also improve empirical coverage and reproducibility documentation. These gains are tempered by inaccurate robustness summaries: Appendix C reverses the equality-error trend, and Section 5 overstates percentage reductions. Table 10's larger-instance cost deterioration is also insufficiently qualified. The retained original evidence and useful additions support a limited net improvement.
